newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Blenheim says could get takeover bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Blenheim says could get takeover bid.

text.p: British exhibitions organiser Blenheim Group Plc said on Tuesday it had received approaches which could lead to an offer following a dawn raid by Dutch publisher VNU, which snapped up 14.99 percent of its shares.

Blenheim said in a statement the approaches were from parties other than VNU, adding it was "continuing to pursue these approaches and a further announcement will be made at the earliest opportunity".

VNU said the stake in Blenheim, which it bought at a price of 500 pence per share from institutional investors, was a strategic long-term investment and that it had no current intention of making an offer for the company.
Blenheim said it had been aware of VNU's interest in the company but had not encouraged its action. The company's shares closed at 460.5 pence, up 25 pence.
VNU said the move was part of an expansion strategy.
"A significant investment in such an exhibitions business is...in line with our long-term strategy of expanding in professional information markets," VNU chairman Bart Brentjens said in a statement.
Exhibitions and conference organising currently account for a scant one percent of VNU group turnover.
Subsidiaries active in this segment are Bill Communications of the U.S. and VNU Business Publications in Britain.
VNU said it was not weighing a short-term bid for all outstanding Blenheim shares, barring rival offers for the firm.
"The acquisition of this stake fits with our strategy to expand our spread of activities in other types of media and other geographical areas," VNU spokesman Maarten Schikker said.
Blenheim was a highly internationally-oriented company with attractive gross margins, he added.
The exhibitions organiser had a significant presence in France, the United States, Britain and Germany, covering 14 different market sectors. Its gross margin in 1995 was 21 percent, Schikker said.
Schikker declined to comment on how far VNU was prepared to build up its newly-acquired stake in Blenheim or whether it planned eventually to take over the company.
"That's a difficult question to answer at this moment. We will consider our position in the near future," he said.
VNU said the 500 pence per share price was full but fair.
"We think this is a full price," Schikker conceded, adding "we are prepared to pay five pounds ($7.8) (per share) to secure a long-term holding in Blenheim. It is a fair price."
"We believe this a very good deal," he added.
